growth_005:n1.prompt:
You are helping me create a transactional email account with {{vendor}} (the chosen email-API provider) so I can send password resets, receipts, and notifications. Before starting, ask me for: my company/legal name, my domain, a contact email and phone number to use on the signup form, my primary use case description (e.g., transactional email for password resets and receipts), and which {{vendor}} I've chosen if not already specified.

Then:
1. Open {{vendor}}'s signup page and fill in all the form fields you can using the details I provide — company name, domain, use case, developer/technical contact info, and any other non-payment fields.
2. Identify which plan/tier supports real deliveries to actual users on a free or trial basis (not just sandbox/demo mode), and note its limits.
3. Locate and summarize the quickstart/integration guide for my primary language, confirming it covers signup-to-first-delivered-email in a copy-paste-complete way; flag anything that seems to require undocumented setup.
4. Prepare a short checklist showing: the plan I should select, the fields already filled in, what payment/billing info will be needed, and where the Terms of Service acceptance appears in the flow.
5. Do NOT enter any payment/billing details, and do NOT click accept on any Terms of Service or submit the form yourself — creating the account is a binding commercial commitment that requires an authorized human.

Stop for human sign-off once the form is pre-filled and the checklist is ready, so I can personally enter billing details and accept the terms.

Report back with: the pre-filled form state or a summary of fields completed, the selected plan and its free-tier/trial deliverability limits, a link or summary of the quickstart guide, and a clear list of what remains for me to do manually (payment entry and ToS acceptance).

growth_005:n2.prompt:
You are helping me authenticate our sending domain with {{vendor}} for transactional email (password resets, receipts, notifications). If you don't already know it, ask me for: (1) my sending domain name, (2) which DNS provider/host manages that domain's records, and (3) confirmation of which {{vendor}} account/workspace to use (assume I have configured credentials already).

Steps to perform:
1. Using {{vendor}}'s domain authentication feature (dashboard or API), initiate authentication for my domain and retrieve the exact SPF, DKIM, and DMARC DNS records it generates — do not invent record values, use only what {{vendor}} outputs.
2. Prepare a clear checklist showing each DNS record (type, host/name, value) that needs to be added at my DNS provider.
3. Do NOT add or modify any DNS records yourself. Present the full checklist and record set to me and then stop for human sign-off, since a human must explicitly approve before any DNS changes are applied.
4. Once I confirm the records have been added (or ask you to proceed after approval), poll {{vendor}}'s verification status endpoint or dashboard periodically to check whether SPF/DKIM/DMARC verification has succeeded. This is an async step — verification may take time to propagate, so note that you may need to check back rather than expecting instant confirmation.
5. Report back with: the exact DNS records generated, current verification status (pending/verified/failed) for each record type, and next steps if verification fails (e.g., record mismatch, propagation delay).

Done looks like: all SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records show as verified in {{vendor}}'s domain status, and you've reported that status to me clearly, noting any records still pending.

growth_005:n3.prompt:
You are helping me prepare the DNS changes needed to authenticate our transactional email (sent via SendGrid) using {{vendor}} as our DNS/edge platform. If you don't already know them, ask me for: (1) my domain name, (2) confirmation that you have configured credentials to read (not modify yet) DNS records in {{vendor}}, and (3) the SPF and DKIM record values SendGrid's domain authentication page provides for our domain (host, record type, and value for each).

Actions:
1. Retrieve or ask me for the exact SPF and DKIM record values SendGrid requires for domain authentication.
2. Check our current DNS records in {{vendor}} for this domain to see if an SPF record already exists (to avoid duplicates/conflicts) and note any existing entries that would need merging.
3. Prepare a precise list of the DNS records to be added or changed — record type, host/name, value, and TTL — formatted so they can be entered directly into {{vendor}}'s dashboard or created via its API.
4. Note if {{vendor}} needs to also handle TLS certificate issuance or custom domain attachment for any related service endpoints, and flag that as informational only.
5. Do not create, edit, or delete any DNS records yet.

Done looks like: a clear, reviewed draft listing every DNS record needed (SPF, DKIM, and any conflict resolution), with any existing conflicting records called out explicitly, ready for me to approve.

Report back with: the full list of proposed DNS records in a simple table (type, host, value, TTL), any conflicts found in current {{vendor}} DNS settings, and a one-line summary of what SPF and DKIM each accomplish. Then stop for human sign-off — do not apply, submit, or create any records in {{vendor}} until I explicitly approve the change.

growth_005:n4.prompt:
You are helping me create transactional email templates using {{vendor}}, the email-API platform I've selected for password resets, receipts, and notifications. If you don't already know it, ask me for: (1) the {{vendor}} account credentials context (assume I have configured credentials already), (2) the list of transactional email types I need (e.g., password reset, receipt, welcome, notification), and (3) any existing copy, branding, or design assets for each email type.

Please do the following:
1. For each email type, draft the template content — subject line, body copy, and merge-field placeholders (e.g., {{user_name}}, {{amount}}, {{reset_link}}) — using {{vendor}}'s documented templating language (merge fields, conditionals, loops as needed).
2. Prefer authoring templates as code if {{vendor}} supports a first-party maintained framework (e.g., React Email, MJML, or equivalent); otherwise use {{vendor}}'s native template editor/language, and keep source files organized so they can be version-controlled.
3. Use {{vendor}}'s template management API or dashboard to create each template as a draft (do not publish or activate live sends yet), noting the template ID/name for each.
4. Generate a test/preview render of each template with sample merge-field data to confirm layout and personalization work correctly.
5. Compile a summary checklist showing: template name, purpose, merge fields used, preview status, and template ID.

Done looks like: all required transactional templates exist in {{vendor}} as drafts, each with a working preview and documented merge fields, plus my checklist ready for review.

Because a human must explicitly approve before changes are applied, do not activate, publish, or trigger any live sends — stop for human sign-off once drafts and the checklist are ready, and report back the template list, IDs, and preview status for my review.

growth_005:n5.prompt:
You are helping me test transactional email delivery for my {{vendor}} account before wiring it into password resets, receipts, and notifications. Use my configured credentials for {{vendor}}; if you don't already know my {{vendor}} API key/config location, domain, or sender address, ask me for them first.

Goal: confirm that a test email can be sent and tracked end-to-end without risking real delivery, using {{vendor}}'s sandbox/test mode or test API key if available.

Steps:
1. Check whether {{vendor}} offers a sandbox domain, test mode, or a dedicated test API key/token that accepts messages and fires events without delivering live mail. Use it if present.
2. Send a single test email via {{vendor}}'s send-email API (or dashboard test-send feature) to a test address I confirm with you, using minimal required fields (from, to, subject, body).
3. Capture the message ID returned in the response.
4. Query {{vendor}}'s per-message event/history API using that message ID to check delivery status (queued, delivered, bounced, etc.).
5. If {{vendor}} supports webhooks for delivered/bounced/complained events, check whether a webhook endpoint is already configured; if not, note that as a follow-up rather than configuring a new receiving endpoint yourself unless I've already set one up and given you its details.
6. Note any open/click tracking data returned for the test message.

Done looks like: you've sent one test email through {{vendor}}, received a message ID, confirmed via the API that the message was accepted/delivered (or reported the actual status if it failed or bounced), and surfaced any event/tracking data available.

Report back: the message ID, the delivery status you observed, whether sandbox/test mode was used, any tracking/event data returned, and any gaps (e.g., no webhook configured yet) I should address next. Do not send any test emails to real customer addresses.
